analysis.one_liner: Requires large employer health plans to cover mental illness on equal terms with medical care.
analysis.headline: Backed by 66 of 100 senators and approved by the Senate's health committee, the bill was placed on the Senate calendar but never came up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop employer health plans from charging higher deductibles, copays, and visit limits for mental illness than for physical illness. It applies to large employers but exempts businesses with 2 to 50 employees, and it does not force any plan to offer mental health coverage in the first place. It also leaves insurers free to manage mental health care through preauthorization and medical-necessity review.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families with coverage from larger employers, who today can face much higher out-of-pocket costs and stricter visit limits for depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and other mental illnesses than for physical ailments. The bill covers all conditions listed in the DSM-IV and includes annual and lifetime spending caps within the limits that must be equalized, so people with severe illness would no longer see their coverage run out early.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans from imposing treatment limits or financial requirements (deductibles, coinsurance, copays, annual and lifetime caps) on mental illness unless comparable limits apply to medical and surgical care
Covers all categories of mental health conditions listed in the DSM-IV, not just a short list of severe diagnoses
Exempts only small employers with 2 to 50 employees, so workers at large and mid-size firms get the protection
Preserves stronger state parity laws and directs the GAO to study the law's effects on insurance costs, access, and quality

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor large group plans and the insurers that administer them would face higher claims costs from equalizing mental health coverage, likely passed through as higher premiums shared with workers. Insurers and employers argued this cost pressure could push some plans to drop mental health benefits entirely, since the bill does not require plans to offer them.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require a plan to offer mental health benefits at all, so a plan facing higher costs under parity could avoid the mandate by dropping the coverage entirely
Plans do not have to provide mental health benefits at parity for out-of-network providers, leaving a gap for patients who cannot find an in-network therapist or psychiatrist
Substance abuse and chemical dependency treatment is expressly excluded from the parity requirement
Cost is the strongest good-faith objection: equalizing mental health coverage raises premiums, and employers and insurers warned the increase could be significant enough to affect coverage decisions

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For millions of people with serious mental illness, the bill's benefit — no more double deductibles, extra copays, or early benefit caps — is substantial and direct. The costs are real but bounded: the small-employer exemption, the freedom to manage care, and the out-of-network carve-out were all designed to blunt employer and insurer cost objections, and the trade-off is that these same loopholes could let some plans drop mental health coverage altogether. On balance the bill is a targeted, incremental parity rule rather than a sweeping mandate, and its costs fall mostly on the parties that shape benefit design.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's health committee approved it and put it on the Senate calendar, but no floor vote was ever scheduled before the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 15, 2001 by Senator Pete Domenici of New Mexico with an original roster of cosponsors spanning both parties, including Senator Paul Wellstone of Minnesota and Senator Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts
Cosponsorship grew to 66 senators — all 49 Senate Democrats, 16 of 49 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 Independents

The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee held hearings on July 11, 2001, ordered the bill reported favorably on August 1, and formally reported it on September 6 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute

The reported version was broadened from the original with a 2-to-50 employee exemption, explicit protection for insurers' medical management practices, an out-of-network parity exception, and a GAO study requirement
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 153), but no further action was ever taken and no vote occurred before the Congress ended

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the large employers that sponsor group plans came out ahead: they never had to absorb the cost of equalizing mental health coverage, and the weaker 1996 parity standard stayed in force for the rest of the decade.

sides.party_line_note: Support was strikingly bipartisan — all 49 Senate Democrats, 16 of 49 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 Independents signed on, and the bill passed committee with additional views filed rather than in dissent — yet it still never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: The bill would force plans that cover mental illness to charge the same deductibles, copays, and visit limits as for physical illness, ending the practice of stricter mental health cost-sharing. Insurers' cost of covering patients rises precisely where patients' out-of-pocket burden falls.

Self-insured corporate plans are regulated through ERISA and would bear the added cost of equalized coverage in premiums and claims. Their interest in avoiding the mandate ran against workers who need mental health care.

The bill would constrain financial limits on mental health care but expressly preserves insurers' utilization review, preauthorization, and network management, so the carve-out industry keeps its gatekeeper role while losing some of the harshest caps.
Small employers are exempt from the mandate, sparing them compliance costs, but the exemption also leaves their workers outside the parity protections.
